accuracy.evidence: Checked against the English national curriculum Appendix 2 (Year 2: commas to separate items in a list) and Common Core L.1.2c (commas in dates and to separate single words in a series) and L.5.2a (punctuation to separate items in a series). The lesson treats the serial or Oxford comma as an accepted style choice, so the lab and mastery mark both forms correct and only ask for consistency.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the named slips: a comma after every word that splits noun phrases (chocolate, cake), a comma before the list starts (I bought, apples), a comma straight after and, a comma after the last item before the verb, a comma in a list of two (cats, and dogs), and leaving out the final and. Each gap role in the lab (need, opt, two, before, and, inside, last, no) has its own message.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagcomma lets learners tap gaps in a sentence to add or remove list commas while a reader-sees chip panel counts the items a reader would pick out, then pack a lunch box by dragging foods and cycling each join through none, comma, and, and comma-and, then fix three sentences that each hide one slip. No other flagship lab punctuates lists, and the shingle gate passed against all flagship labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: The chip panel shows the effect of each comma: apples pears plums and grapes reads as one long thing, then splits into four chips as commas go in, and chocolate, cake wrongly becomes two foods. Learners see why a comma belongs after a whole item and why two items only need and, before the done message states the rule.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting distractors: where the commas go in the fruit list (after every word), whether chocolate cake needs a comma inside it, and whether cats and dogs needs a comma. Each is tested in the very next task and echoed in the done message with the reason.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Challenge questions rotate answer order, and each wrong option carries a tagged explanation that names the slip, such as a comma never splits an item or two things just need and. Wrong taps in the lab explain the role of that gap rather than only marking it wrong.

readability.evidence: Learner audience gates pass: kid paragraphs score FK 2.5 with short sentences and familiar foods and pets as examples; adult paragraphs score FK 5.2 while keeping the terms list, series, noun phrase, conjunction and serial comma.

no_filler.evidence: Content gate passed with no filler phrases and low overlap with other lessons. Every paragraph carries a rule, a worked example or a named mistake, and practice explanations count the commas from the number of items rather than restating the answer.

mobile.evidence: Walkthrough passed on iPhone 13 and desktop: every Show me completes within the limit, gap targets are widened for fingers, chip columns adapt to narrow screens, sentences do not wrap before a join, and the pack buttons name each food so the task works without dragging.

accessibility.evidence: axe-core reports no violations in light or dark theme. The canvas aria-label is updated with each message, every gap and food has a labelled button alternative, text colours come from the theme palette with contrast checked in both modes, and timers respect reduced motion.

sources: DfE (2013) English programmes of study: key stages 1 and 2, English Appendix 2: Vocabulary, grammar and punctuation (Year 2)
Common Core State Standards for English Language Arts (2010) L.1.2c, L.5.2a
DfE (2023) English grammar, punctuation and spelling test framework, key stage 2
